1:
Delitzsch alone names a battle. The psalm shares with its neighbour "not only the thought of the kingly exaltation of Jahve over the peoples of the earth, but also its historical occasion, viz., Jehoshaphat's victory over the allied neighbouring nations, — a victory without a conflict, and consequently all the more manifestly a victory of Jahve". The trumpet, he adds, makes this "the proper new year's" psalm. Calvin dismisses the temple dedication as "a conjecture which has little to support it", supposing the psalm delivered to the Levites "before the temple was built, and when the ark as yet abode in the tabernacle". Clarke dates it to "the happy state of the Jews when returned to their own land"; Gill refers it all to Christ's ascension.

Augustine takes the title instead, reading the sons of Korah through the place of Calvary. The name yields the bald head at which children mocked Elisha, and he makes the mockery a figure: "in the place of Calvary, crucifying Christ, and lifting on the Cross, they said as it were with childish sense, Go up, thou bald head. For what is, Go up? Crucify Him." The bears acted "not so much in cruelty as in mystery" — hence, "let none mock the Cross of Christ."

Who is summoned is read three ways at once. Henry allows both: "all you people" is either Israel, over whom the psalmist had influence, or "all you people and nations of the earth", making the verse "a prophecy of the conversion of the Gentiles". Clarke divides the reasons rather than the audience: "the Jews, for being delivered from the Babylonish captivity; the Gentiles, for being called to enter into the glorious liberty". Spurgeon lets Israel "lead the van"; Gill means the Gentiles.

The clapping is traced to a coronation. Ellicott cites the hand-clapping at the crowning of a king: with the Hebrews, "as with our own English forefathers, this sign of popular assent... played a large and important part". Both preachers then defend the noise. Henry answers the objection before it is made: such expressions "as to some may seem indecent and imprudent ought not to be hastily censured, much less ridiculed", since "God will accept the strength of the affection and excuse the weakness of the expressions." Spurgeon agrees that "our joy in God may be demonstrative, and yet he will not censure it", and finds a universal language in the gesture: "if they cannot all speak the same tongue, the symbolic language of the hands they can all use."

Calvin argues that the deliverance must be Israel's: had God "erected among the Gentiles some formidable kingdom, this would rather have deprived all of their courage than given them matter to sing and leap for joy." Spurgeon turns the terribleness the same way: "omnipotence, which is terrible to crush, is almighty to protect."

On the subduing they differ over tense and sense. Clarke "would rather read this in the past tense, relative to what God did for their fathers"; Gill reports that the Jews expect a literal subjection of the Gentiles, "but these, and all other expressions of the like kind, are to be understood in a spiritual sense"; Wesley reads the "us" as the church.

What the chosen inheritance is divides them again. Ellicott suspects the pronoun: the Septuagint read "his inheritance", suggesting it originally ran "He chooses us for His inheritance, an even commoner thought in the Hebrew mind". He takes the excellency of Jacob, "literally the loftiness of Jacob", to mean the country, the phrase covering elsewhere the national glory, the Temple, and even "the pride of Jacob". Wesley makes it "the presence and worship, and blessing of God"; Spurgeon makes it God himself — "he was the boast and glory of Israel, he is and shall be ours" — and concludes: "we submit our will, our choice, our desire, wholly to him."
5:
Where God goes up to is the question of the tile, and Ellicott answers it from the noise: the going up is "not... to heaven, but... to the Temple, as is shown by the public acclaim accompanying the ark to its resting-place after victory." Delitzsch reads it the same way, the ascent presupposing a descent: God "has come down to fight on behalf of His people", so that "they return to the Holy City and He to His throne". Gill will have only the other sense: the Son of God went up "from earth to heaven in human nature, really, locally, and visibly, in the sight of his apostles". Spurgeon supplies the scene — "the fight is over, the conqueror ascends to his triumphal chariot" — and asks: "He came not without song, shall we imagine that he returned in silence?"

The middle positions keep both. Clarke gives the order: "primarily, this may refer to the rejoicing and sounding of trumpets, when the ark was lifted up to be carried on the shoulders of the Levites. But it is generally understood as a prophetic declaration of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ." Wesley says it in a line: the verse is "meant literally of the ark: but mystically of Christ's ascension". Henry gives both too.

The repeated command draws different counts and the same conclusion. Clarke observes that the word "is four times repeated in this short verse, and shows at once the earnestness and happiness of the people"; Spurgeon counts five across the two verses. Henry reads the repetition as a rebuke to our slowness — "so backward are we to this duty that we have need to be urged to it by precept upon precept" — and defends the reuse: "we may sing praises again and again in the same words, and it is no vain repetition if it be done with new affections." Ellicott, as usual, corrects the verb rather than expounding it: "better, strike the harp."

Then comes the psalm's own qualification, and it splits the tile cleanly. Ellicott takes it musically: "rather, play a fine tune", or perhaps, with the ancient versions, "play with skill". Everyone else takes it of the mind. Clarke translates "sing an instructive song" and lays down the rule: "let sense and sound go together... Understand what you sing; and feel what you understand" — hence the flat verdict, "multitudes sing foolishly." Henry distinguishes two duties in the word: to sing "intelligently, as those that do yourselves understand why and for what reasons you praise God", and "instructively, as those that desire to make others understand God's glorious perfections" — behind both, "it is not an acceptable service if it be not a reasonable service." Wesley asks only that it be done "not formally and carelessly, but seriously".

Spurgeon turns the same requirement into an attack on church music — "sing a didactic Psalm. Sound doctrine praises God" — and finds two opposite faults. From "the slovenly way in which some make a noise in singing" it appears "they fancy any sound will do"; while "from the great attention paid by some to the mere music, we feel sadly sure that the sense has no effect upon them." The charge is blunt: "is it not a sin to be tickling men's ears with sounds when we profess to be adoring the Lord? What has a sensuous delight in organs, anthems, etc., to do with devotion?"

On the kingship of all the earth Wesley says only that it is not ours alone, and Clarke that God "has no limited power, no confined dominion". Spurgeon uses it against a narrower hope: the Jews of the Saviour's time "resented this truth, but had their hearts been right they would have rejoiced in it", since they "would have kept their God to themselves" — "alas! how selfishness turns honey into wormwood."
8:
The reign over the heathen is read as two reigns. Spurgeon draws the distinction sharply: "now at this moment, over the most debased idolaters, God holds a secret rule; here is work for faith. How we ought to long for the day when the rule now unrecognized shall be delighted in!" Clarke says the same with the gospel supplying the change: the dominion is universal already, "yet more is here meant. God reigns over the heathen when, by the preaching of the Gospel, they are brought into the Church of Christ." Gill takes the second reign as begun and unfolding, from the conversions of the first Christian ages to a destruction of Rome still to come.

Where the throne of holiness stands gets three answers from one voice: Clarke locates it in "the heaven of heavens; also the temple at Jerusalem; and, lastly, the hearts of the faithful." Wesley keeps to the first, heaven being "often called God's throne, whence God is said to behold and to rule all nations". Spurgeon describes the seat rather than its place: it is "an undisputed throne, whose decrees, acts, and commands are holiness itself", never "stained with injustice, or defiled with sin" — its occupant sitting "in serenity, for he knows his own power, and sees that his purposes will not miscarry."

Who the gathered princes are is the tile's real dispute, and it turns on a single Hebrew word. Clarke reads it as willingness rather than rank: they are "the voluntary people — the princely, noble, or free-willed people; those who gladly receive the word of life", noble as the Bereans were, who "searched the Scriptures to see whether these things were so". Gill reports the same rendering as an alternative, "the willing" or "voluntary ones of his people". Delitzsch keeps both senses at once, the word carrying "the twofold meaning of generosi". Spurgeon and Wesley take actual rulers: "nobles bow their willing necks to his sway", and "their great men shall be good men, their royal ones regenerate ones".

On whose people they become, Clarke argues from the covenant's date: "Who were Abraham's people? Not the Jews; the covenant was made with him while yet in uncircumcision. Properly speaking, the Gentiles are those whom he represented" — "the Gentiles who, receiving the Gospel, are made partakers of the faith of Abraham." Wesley finds the same point in the phrasing: the psalm "doth not say the people of Abraham, lest this should be appropriated to the Israelites; but the people of the God of Abraham, whether they be Jews or Gentiles." Delitzsch says the promise about the nations blessed in the patriarch's seed "is being fulfilled"; Gill notes that the princes are gathered "not against Christ, as at his first coming, but to him".

The shields divide the grammarians from the preachers. Ellicott identifies them with "the princes just mentioned", and notes that the ancient versions, rendering "strong ones", make those the subject of the verb — so that on their reading it is the princes, not God, who "have been mightily exalted". Clarke reports the same Latin rendering, "the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted", supposed to mean rulers of provinces present at the temple's dedication, but declines it: the words "refer to something by which the inhabitants of the earth are defended; God's providence, guardian angels", and "great as secular rulers are, God is greater".

Spurgeon closes on the gathering. The prophetic eye "sees the willing subjects of the great King assembled to celebrate his glory": "how august will be the parliament where the Lord Jesus shall open the court, and princes shall rise up to do him honour!" The God once "known only to here and there a patriarch" shall be "adored by a seed as many as the stars of heaven", and "Babel's dispersion shall be obliterated by the gathering arm of the Great Shepherd King."
